script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for November 06, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - Remimazolam versus propofol for sedation in mechanically venti
sentences: Story 1 is about Remimazolam versus propofol for sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials..
This is a systematic review / meta-analysis from Journal of critical care.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in ICU patients, how should we interpret Remimazolam compared with propofol for sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials?
Six RCTs including 705 patients were analyzed.
No statistically significant difference was detected in the percentage of time within the target sedation range (MD, -0.45%; 95% CI, -2.46 to 1.55; p = 0.56; I2 = 0%).

No significant differences were detected in sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, ICU length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation, or safety outcomes, although several estimates were imprecise.
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: Use this for journal club before practice change; decide whether the measured outcome is important enough for bedside decisions.

articles.title: Remimazolam versus propofol for sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.summary: Continuous endpoints were reported using mean differences (MDs), and dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RRs), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Six RCTs including 705 patients were analyzed. No statistically significant difference was detected in the percentage of time within the target sedation range (MD, -0.45%; 95% CI, -2.46 to 1.55; p = 0.56; I2 = 0%). No significant differences were detected in sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, ICU length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation, or safety outcomes, although several estimates were imprecise. Propofol is widely used for sedation in the intensive care unit (ICU), but its use may be limited by cardiovascular depression, hypertriglyceridemia, and propofol infusion syndrome.

articles.title: Consensus on a core outcome set for ventilation trials in critically ill patients with acute brain injury: results of an international Delphi consensus study.
articles.summary: Inclusion required >70% rating as "critical" (score 7-9) and ≤15% as "not important" (1-3). 78 stakeholders participated in Round 1; 60 completed all rounds (23.1% attrition). Three outcomes were not ratified due to disease-specificity (NIH Stroke Scale) or lack of universal applicability (brain death, coma-free days). A 3-level hierarchical composite endpoint was ratified at Consensus Meeting 2: (1) intensive care unit survival, (2) no reintubation within 72 hours, and (3) days alive without mechanical ventilation. Clinical research evaluating mechanical ventilation liberation in patients with acute brain injury (ABI) shows substantial outcome heterogeneity, limiting evidence synthesis.
